promptText: What is the key operational risk of pinning a production LLM feature to a floating alias like "model-latest" instead of a dated, immutable snapshot?
options: The provider can silently change what the alias resolves to, shifting production behavior with no deploy event or code change on your side to explain or bisect the regression
Floating aliases are always more expensive per token than dated snapshots
Floating aliases cannot be used with streaming responses
Dated snapshots automatically receive safety and quality improvements that floating aliases do not
explanation: A floating alias always points to whatever the provider currently considers latest, so behavior can change with zero deploy events on your side, unlike a pinned dated snapshot which stays fixed until you explicitly change it.

promptText: Why should a system prompt edit go through the same review and evaluation-gate process as an application code change, rather than being edited live in a dashboard?
options: A prompt template directly controls model behavior for every request that uses it, so a small wording change can alter tone, correctness, or safety behavior as significantly as a code change, and an unversioned edit cannot be attributed or rolled back with confidence
Dashboards are technically incapable of storing text longer than a few sentences
Prompt edits only affect the model's token cost, never its actual output behavior
Review is required purely for legal compliance reasons, not because prompt changes affect behavior
explanation: A prompt is a first-class production artifact with real behavioral blast radius; without a version identifier and evaluation gate, a regression it causes is undebuggable and unattributable, exactly like an unreviewed code change.

promptText: In the canary/shadow rollout pipeline described for LLM changes, what happens during the 'shadow deployment' stage specifically?
options: The candidate receives a mirrored copy of real production traffic and is scored for comparison, but its responses are never actually shown to users
The candidate is shown to exactly 50% of real users immediately after passing the offline evaluation gate
The candidate only runs against synthetic traffic generated by another LLM, never real production requests
The candidate replaces the production version entirely but only during off-peak hours
explanation: Shadow deployment mirrors real traffic to the candidate purely for scoring and comparison with zero user-facing risk, since nothing it produces is ever actually served to a real user.

promptText: Why is detecting a vendor-initiated (silent) model change fundamentally different from detecting a regression caused by your own team's deploy?
options: There is no deploy event in your own change log to anchor an investigation to, so detection must come from continuously probing the live model's output against a historical baseline rather than watching your own deployment history
Vendor-initiated changes are always announced in advance via email, so detection is actually easier
Vendor-initiated changes never affect evaluation scores, only latency
Your own team's deploys cannot be detected at all without vendor cooperation
explanation: A vendor-side model swap behind a stable alias produces a behavior shift with zero corresponding entries in your own deployment log, so a scheduled drift probe comparing live outputs against a stored baseline is required to catch it.

promptText: Why should an in-flight, multi-turn conversation session NOT be force-switched to a new model/prompt version the instant a rollout or rollback happens?
options: Switching mid-conversation can produce jarring, self-contradicting behavior, such as the assistant forgetting a tool it just offered or contradicting something it said a turn earlier under a different version's contract
Force-switching is technically impossible due to API rate limits
Force-switching would violate data residency requirements in every jurisdiction
In-flight sessions are always billed at a fixed rate regardless of which version serves them
explanation: A session pinned to the version active at its start should drain naturally to completion, because forcibly switching an in-flight session's underlying prompt/model contract can break continuity with what was already said earlier in the conversation.

promptText: What is the core purpose of an LLM/prompt version registry in a production architecture?
options: It serves as the single source of truth for which model pin, prompt template, and configuration are currently live for each feature, with lifecycle state and linked evaluation results, so services resolve versions from it rather than hardcoding strings
It exists purely to cache LLM API responses to reduce cost
It replaces the need for any evaluation gate since registered versions are assumed correct by default
It only stores model weights, never prompt templates or configuration
explanation: The registry is the authoritative record of what is running in production right now and what proved it belonged there, enabling attribution, rollback, and audit rather than tribal knowledge scattered across dashboards and config files.

promptText: Why is rolling back a bad LLM prompt/model version fundamentally different from rolling back a bad application code deploy, even setting aside the stateful-conversation issue?
options: A code rollback is deterministic and exact -- the next request is served identically to before; an LLM rollback only shifts the distribution of likely outputs back toward what it was, so the rolled-back state must be re-validated against the evaluation gate rather than trusted on faith
LLM rollbacks are always slower to execute than code rollbacks because they require retraining
Code rollbacks require a canary stage while LLM rollbacks never do
There is no meaningful difference; both are deterministic and require no re-validation
explanation: Because an LLM system is probabilistic, 'the version that used to work' is a claim about an output distribution, not a guaranteed specific response -- so a rollback needs re-validation against the evaluation gate, unlike a deterministic code rollback.

promptText: A candidate prompt version scores 0.89 faithfulness versus production's 0.86 on 300 evaluated examples, and their 95% confidence intervals overlap substantially. What is the correct interpretation and next step?
options: The difference is well within the range noise alone could produce; promoting on this evidence alone would be shipping a coin flip dressed as a data-driven decision, so the canary stage should be extended to collect more samples or run a formal significance test
Since 0.89 is numerically larger than 0.86, the candidate should be promoted to 100% traffic immediately
Overlapping confidence intervals prove the candidate is definitely worse and should be rejected outright
Confidence intervals are irrelevant to promotion decisions; only the raw score difference matters
explanation: Overlapping confidence intervals mean the observed difference is not strong evidence of a real improvement given the sampling noise inherent in LLM-judge scores; the correct action is to gather more evidence before promoting or rejecting.

promptText: How does a drift-probe mechanism for detecting silent vendor-side model changes differ structurally from Chapter 68-style production monitoring?
options: The drift probe runs a small, fixed set of reference prompts on a schedule directly against the model, independent of real user traffic, so it can isolate model-only behavior shifts, whereas production monitoring samples live, varying real traffic
The drift probe and production monitoring are identical mechanisms with different names
The drift probe only checks latency and cost, never quality scores
Production monitoring runs less frequently than drift probes because it is more expensive per request
explanation: Because production traffic varies and passes through your own prompt/application layer, a fixed, unchanging probe set run independently and directly against the model is needed to isolate a change to the model itself, bypassing confounds from traffic mix or your own code changes.

promptText: Why does classical champion/challenger deployment (from pre-LLM MLOps) need to be adapted, rather than applied unchanged, for comparing two LLM versions?
options: Classical champion/challenger compares models against a well-defined ground-truth label (like an actual chargeback outcome); LLM systems have no equivalent real-time ground truth, so the comparison must use reference-free LLM-as-judge scores and a statistical hypothesis test instead of a simple accuracy comparison
Champion/challenger cannot be applied to LLMs at all because LLMs never receive real traffic during evaluation
LLM challengers must always be smaller models than the champion, unlike classical ML challengers
Champion/challenger requires retraining the champion model on every comparison, which LLM providers do not allow
explanation: Classical fraud/credit-risk models had objective ground-truth labels available in real time; LLM output quality is judged via reference-free metrics, so the promotion decision becomes a statistical significance test over noisy scores rather than a hard accuracy comparison.

promptText: Why is 'prompt-as-code' (storing templates in version control, reviewed via pull requests, tested in CI) described as foundational to almost every other LLMOps capability?
options: You cannot roll back a prompt you never versioned, cannot gate a change on evaluation results without a discrete versioned change to gate, and cannot answer an audit question about what generated a past response without a captured, distinct version
Prompt-as-code is required because LLM APIs reject any prompt not stored in a git repository
It is only a stylistic convention with no functional dependency from other LLMOps capabilities
It matters solely because it reduces the number of tokens a prompt consumes
explanation: Versioning, gating, rollback, and audit traceability all presuppose that a prompt change is a discrete, identifiable, retrievable artifact -- which is exactly what prompt-as-code provides and an inline dashboard edit does not.

promptText: What distinguishes a canary rollout from a true A/B test, even though both route a fraction of traffic to a variant?
options: A canary is a risk-mitigation mechanism designed to end quickly in full promotion or full rollback once confidence is reached; an A/B test is a measurement mechanism run for a pre-planned duration and sample size regardless of early trends, specifically to avoid stopping on noise
A canary always requires a larger traffic percentage than an A/B test
A/B tests are only used for evaluating cost, never for evaluating output quality
Canary rollouts and A/B tests are simply two names for the exact same process
explanation: A canary is used to confirm a candidate is not broken and quickly decide promote-or-rollback, while a genuine A/B test compares two plausible permanent variants over a pre-registered duration to avoid the false-positive risk of stopping early on a favorable-looking trend.

promptText: A production system wants a canary evaluation with a margin of error of plus-or-minus 2 percentage points around an expected pass rate of 0.90. Using n approximately equal to z^2 * p(1-p) / E^2, roughly how many evaluated examples are needed, and what is the practical implication for a canary that only reaches 50-100 scored examples?
options: Roughly 864 examples are needed; a canary reaching only 50-100 examples cannot responsibly resolve a difference this small, so the acceptable effect size must be widened or the canary stage extended until enough traffic accumulates
Roughly 50 examples are needed, so a canary of 50-100 examples is already more than sufficient
Sample size is irrelevant to margin of error once the pass rate exceeds 0.85
Exactly 300 examples are always sufficient for any margin of error, since that was the example used elsewhere in the chapter
explanation: Plugging z=1.96, p=0.90, E=0.02 into n = z^2*p(1-p)/E^2 gives roughly 864 -- far more than a 50-100 example canary can supply, meaning that small a sample cannot reliably resolve a 2-point difference, so the promotion decision must wait for more accumulated evidence.

promptText: An organization runs a dozen AI features sharing the same foundation model provider. Why is a per-feature, decentralized drift-detection approach (each team independently referencing model identifiers and independently watching for drift) structurally worse than a centralized, org-wide drift-detection design?
options: A single upstream vendor model update could regress all twelve features simultaneously, but with decentralized detection each team might independently and slowly rediscover the same root cause in isolation, with no mechanism connecting the dots across teams or immediately surfacing every affected downstream feature
Decentralized detection is actually always faster because each team has more context on its own feature's traffic patterns
Centralized drift detection is only useful for cost tracking, not for correctness or safety issues
There is no meaningful difference in outcome between centralized and decentralized drift detection at any organizational scale
explanation: Centralizing model-version resolution and running drift probes against every distinct model pin, tagged by which features depend on it, means one detected drift event immediately surfaces every downstream feature it could affect, rather than twelve teams separately and slowly discovering the same shared upstream cause.

promptText: A regulated-industry audit requires proving exactly which model version and prompt template generated a specific customer-facing response from six months ago. Which combination of practices would make this traceability chain irrecoverably broken?
options: Resolving 'current production version' freshly at request time without persisting which version was actually returned, editing prompt templates in place rather than versioning them, and relying on a floating model alias with no logged record of what it resolved to on that day
Tagging every response at generation time with the exact model pin and prompt template version, and retaining retired versions and their evaluation history in the registry
Storing every prompt template in version control with pull-request review before it reaches production
Pinning every conversational session to the exact version set active at its start and logging which version served which turn
explanation: Each of the listed failures destroys traceability: without persisting the resolved version at generation time, in-place template edits erasing prior text, or floating aliases with no logged resolution history, there is no way to reconstruct after the fact exactly what generated a past response -- the other three options are exactly the practices that preserve auditability.
